decision.explanation: Divide by 4 to get z^2+z=3. Completing the square gives (z+1/2)^2=13/4, so p+q=1/2+13/4=15/4. Taking square roots gives z=(-1±√13)/2.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: The equation $4{z}^{2}+4z=12$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+4z & =12 \\ 4({z}^{2}+z) & =12 \\ {z}^{2}+z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\cdot z+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=\frac{1}{2},q=\frac{13}{4},$ and $p+q=\frac{15}{4}.$ 

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}} \\ |z+\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =\frac{-1\pm \sqrt{13}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation 4z2+4z=12 can be written in the form (z+p)2=q. Find p+q, and solve the equation.

a
p+q=134,z=−1±132
b
p+q=114,z=3±112
c
p+q=154,z=−1±132
d
p+q=154,z=1±112
e
p+q=174,z=−3±112
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side. 4z2+4z=124(z2+z)=12z2+z=3z2+2⋅12⋅z=3z2+2⋅(12)⋅z+(12)2−(12)2=3(z+12)2−(12)2=3

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

(z+12)2−(12)2=3(z+12)2−14=124(z+12)2=134

So, p=12,q=134, and p+q=154.

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

(z+12)2=134|z+12|=132z+12=±132z=−12±132z=−1±132

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Positive Leading Coefficient
content.problem: The equation $4{z}^{2}+4z=12$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+4z & =12 \\ 4({z}^{2}+z) & =12 \\ {z}^{2}+z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\cdot z+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=\frac{1}{2},q=\frac{13}{4},$ and $p+q=\frac{15}{4}.$ 

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}} \\ |z+\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =\frac{-1\pm \sqrt{13}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Multiplying by −1 gives 20x²−60x+41=0. Completing the square gives 20(x−3/2)²=4, so q=4. Thus x=3/2±√(4/20)=3/2±√5/5.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: The equation $-20{x}^{2}+60x-41=0$ can be written in the form $20(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-20{x}^{2}+60x-41) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x & =-41 \\ 20({x}^{2}-3x) & =-41 \\ 20[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}] & =-41 \\ 20[{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}] & =-41\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-20\cdot \frac{9}{4} & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-45 & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =45-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{4}{20} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

a

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

20x2−60x+41=020x2−60x=−4120(x2−3x)=−4120[x2−2⋅32x+(32)2−(32)2]=−4120[(x−32)2−94]=−41

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

20(x−32)2−20⋅94=−4120(x−32)2−45=−4120(x−32)2=45−4120(x−32)2=4

Therefore, q=4. We now solve the equation using the square root method:

20(x−32)2=4(x−32)2=420(x−32)2=15(x−32)2=15|x−32|=15x−32=±15x−32=±55x=32±55

content.problem: The equation $-20{x}^{2}+60x-41=0$ can be written in the form $20(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-20{x}^{2}+60x-41) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x & =-41 \\ 20({x}^{2}-3x) & =-41 \\ 20[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}] & =-41 \\ 20[{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}] & =-41\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-20\cdot \frac{9}{4} & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-45 & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =45-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{4}{20} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: The equation $2{x}^{2}+10x+12=0$ can be written in the form $2(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side,  factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+10x+12 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}+10x & =-12 \\ 2{x}^{2}+10x & =-12 \\ 2({x}^{2}+5x) & =-12 \\ 2[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{2}x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}] & =-12 \\ 2[{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{4}] & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{25}{4} & =-12 \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{2} & =-12 \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =-12+\frac{25}{2} \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5}{2}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\ |x+\frac{5}{2}| & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x+\frac{5}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{5}{2}\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{6}{3}=-3 \\ x & =-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{4}{2}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-3$ and $x=-2.$

The equation −4w2−16w+9=0 can be written in the form 4(w+p)2=q. Find p, and solve the equation.

a
p=2,w=−92 and w=12
b
p=1,w=−52 and w=12
c
p=2,w=−32 and w=32
d
p=2,w=−12 and w=52
e
p=1,w=−72 and w=1
Submit

decision.explanation: Multiplying by −1 and rearranging gives 4w²+16w=9. Completing the square gives 4(w+2)²=25, so p=2. Thus w=−2±5/2, giving w=−9/2 and w=1/2.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-16w+9=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-16w+9) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+16w-9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+16w-9 & =0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+16w & =9 \\ 4({w}^{2}+4w) & =9 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot w+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}] & =9 \\ 4[{(w+2)}^{2}-4] & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+2)}^{2}-4\cdot 4 & =9 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2}-16 & =9 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2} & =9+16 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=2.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+2)}^{2} & =25 \\ {(w+2)}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(w+2)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |w+2| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ w+2 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ w & =-2\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =-2-\frac{5}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ w & =-2+\frac{5}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $w=-\frac{9}{2}$ and $w=\frac{1}{2}.$

a
p=2,w=−92 and w=12
b
p=1,w=−52 and w=12
c
p=2,w=−32 and w=32

p=2,w=−12 and w=52
e
p=1,w=−72 and w=1

EXPLANATION

First, we multiply the equation by −1: (−1)⋅(−4w2−16w+9)=(−1)⋅04w2+16w−9=0

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

4w2+16w−9=04w2+16w=94(w2+4w)=94[w2+2⋅2⋅w+22−22]=94[(w+2)2−4]=9

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

4(w+2)2−4⋅4=94(w+2)2−16=94(w+2)2=9+164(w+2)2=25

Therefore, p=2. We now solve the equation using the square root method: 4(w+2)2=25(w+2)2=254(w+2)2=254|w+2|=52w+2=±52w=−2±52

We simplify the two solutions: w=−2−52=−92w=−2+52=12

So, the solutions are w=−92 and w=12.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
content.problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-16w+9=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-16w+9) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+16w-9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+16w-9 & =0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+16w & =9 \\ 4({w}^{2}+4w) & =9 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot w+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}] & =9 \\ 4[{(w+2)}^{2}-4] & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+2)}^{2}-4\cdot 4 & =9 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2}-16 & =9 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2} & =9+16 \\ 4{(w+2)}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=2.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+2)}^{2} & =25 \\ {(w+2)}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(w+2)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |w+2| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ w+2 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ w & =-2\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =-2-\frac{5}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ w & =-2+\frac{5}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $w=-\frac{9}{2}$ and $w=\frac{1}{2}.$
